page_placements.theme: Target properties and training history set how deeply unlearning works

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates unlearning effectiveness and extraction strength across training conditions, but does not test the recovery attacks named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The Phi-1.5 TOFU experiment reports Extraction Strength after unlearning, which the paper describes as measuring resistance to extraction attacks. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt variations, nor compare extraction to an unlearned model that never saw the target data. Other reported results concern grokking's effect on unlearning and do not test the specified recovery attacks.
record.test_reason: The study compares how well standard unlearning methods work on grokked versus pre-grokked checkpoints (vision) and on locally grokked versus ungrokked TOFU examples (Phi-1.5). It applies no recovery attack: no relearning, no activation ablation or deletion-versus-blocking analysis, no quantization, and no prompt variation. Its ESunlearn scores are post-unlearning extraction measures with no chance or never-trained reference. They compare training states and do not ask whether unlearning resists attacks. It cites WMDP/RMU and Xu et al. on reversibility but tests neither.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that grokked vision checkpoints and locally grokked TOFU examples permit more effective unlearning with less collateral damage, and more seed-stable unlearning in vision. They attribute this to more modular representations, lower forget/retain gradient correlation and lower local complexity. They present grokking as a conceptual lens rather than a practical recipe.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares pre- and post-grokking training states while applying standard unlearning methods; it does not reproduce a recovery-attack recipe from the cited unlearning papers.
record.method_sensitivity: Unlearning outcomes vary with grokking state, forget-set size, algorithm, architecture, and forget rate; the authors also report that efficiency advantages depend on task difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: In Phi-1.5 on TOFU, locally grokked forget examples reach lower post-unlearning ESunlearn than ungrokked ones across GA, GD, KL, PO and NPO (e.g., GA 0.344 vs 0.518; GD 0.291 vs 0.497). RMU is mixed. In vision, grokked checkpoints show lower forget accuracy and less collateral damage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The model's training state (grokked/well-generalized versus not) affects how deeply standard unlearning removes target data, measured without any recovery attack.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be released upon publication.
record.problems: The language experiment uses one model and a synthetic dataset. The paper gives no chance-level or never-trained reference for the reported Extraction Strength values, and the Table 2 results do not provide numeric uncertainty alongside those values.
record.rows_left_out: Other Table 2 method and forget-set-size results, and the vision-domain unlearning tables, are not separately transcribed here; the selected rows are the numerical ESunlearn comparisons explicitly discussed in the Section 4.2 prose.

untested.parts: Not tested. There is no simple recovery attack, and no chance-level or never-trained reference for forget-set ES.
No relearning attack. Fine-tuning appears only as a vision unlearning baseline.
No activation-direction ablation or deletion-versus-suppression analysis. The gradient, CKA and complexity analyses concern forget/retain entanglement, not recoverability.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context recovery test.
No method is tested against recovery attacks. Grokking is offered as a training-state lever, not as an attack-robust method.

record.verdict_notes: The authors assert that ES measures resistance to extraction attacks, but ESunlearn is just forget-set generation tendency after unlearning; no attack is run. Table 2 text is garbled for the 150 and 200 example columns. The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its limits_scope label on A are not supported, because the study never checks whether forgotten knowledge can be recovered.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison to a model that never saw the target data; no explicit chance-level reference for Extraction Strength; no separate attack variants.
Fine-tuning is used as an unlearning method, not as an attack to recover forgotten knowledge.
No activation-direction ablation or test of blocked access versus deletion.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language change, or in-context recovery test.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the specified recovery attacks.

relation.reason: The only engagement is one clause citing Xu et al. 2025 on 'shallow forgetting that can be reversed', the WMDP citation for RMU, and an unsupported line saying ES shows information 'truly forgotten rather than merely suppressed'. That is citation, not discussion or use of the claim.

tranche.reason: The study runs standard unlearning methods on grokked vs pre-grokked vision models and on locally grokked vs ungrokked TOFU examples (Phi-1.5). It applies no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting attack, so it tests none of versions B to F. ES is not compared with chance or a retrained model, so it does not test version A either.

source_check.notes: Table 2 is garbled in the text but can be rebuilt. ESretain fills 8 columns (Original 0.647-0.649). ESunlearn Originals are 0.597 (50), 0.630 (100), 0.658 (150) and 0.661 (200). The prose confirms the 200-example GA values of 0.398 vs 0.512. The paper reports no recovery attack and no chance or retrained reference. The table shows no standard deviations, so the small RMU margins can't be checked against noise.

statements.correction: GA: 0.344 vs 0.518 at 50 examples. GD: 0.291 vs 0.497 at 100 examples. GA, GD, KL, PO and NPO are lower for grokked at all four sizes (50-200). RMU ESunlearn is lower for grokked at each size, by small margins: 0.560 vs 0.586 (50), 0.551 vs 0.556 (100), 0.291 vs 0.303 (150), 0.110 vs 0.129 (200). The authors call RMU 'more variable' but say it 'generally favors grokked examples'.
statements.problem: The GA and GD pairs and the five-method claim are right. 'RMU mixed' misreads Table 2: RMU ESunlearn is lower for grokked examples at every forget-set size, though by small margins. The authors say RMU 'still generally favors grokked examples'. The statement gives no set sizes, but that is an omission, not an error.
